catalog_citation: Daniels, Don R. 2010. A preliminary phonological history of the Sogeram languages of Papua New Guinea. Oceanic Linguistics 49(1): 163-193. doi:10.1353/ol.0.0068
catalog_locator: sec. 2 PROTO-SOGERAM, p. 168 (the sentence directly after inventory (1)); restated sec. 4.1.2, p. 175 and sec. 4.3.1, p. 177.
catalog_quote: Stress is almost always word-final in the daughter languages, and it was probably also word-final in PSOG. The central vowel /ɨ/ behaves as a neutral vowel in the family, arising paragogically and epenthetically in many situations (cf. 3.1.2, 3.1.4, and 4.4.1), and being the result of any vowel-centering processes (such as 4.1.2. and 5.2.4). [p. 168] ... 4.1.2 Vowel centering (V-R > ɨ / C__C.’σopen). Unrounded vowels in closed penults centered to /ɨ/ when followed by open ultimas; the fact that PSOG probably had word-final stress helps motivate this change. However, it is evidenced in only three cognate sets: PSOG *kimri ‘cold’ > PCS *kɨmri > Manat ɣɨmri, Mum kɨmri; PSOG *tampa ‘stone’ > PCS *tɨmpa > Apalɨ rɨmba, Mum tɨmba; and PSOG *maŋka ‘egg’ > PCS *mɨŋga > Apalɨ maŋgɨ (with vowel metathesis), Sirva mɨŋga. [p. 175] ... While this innovation is not a bizarre phonetic development, the fact that these languages probably had word-final stress makes it a little peculiar. For this reason, I suggest that it originated only once, in PNCS, and spread from there across language and dialect boundaries. As the innovation apparently took place before PNCS split into Mum and Sirva, Manat and PNCS may have been mutually intelligible at the time, and positing the spread of this innovation across their dialect boundary is plausible. [p. 177]

new_statements.relation_note: Language not in the catalog and no existing statements; this is the first placement statement found for Mum. It is a family-wide generalization ('the daughter languages') by the one linguist who collected Mum data, so it is indirect evidence of final stress in Mum rather than a description of Mum prosody.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A family-level statement, not a Mum-specific one: stress falls on the last syllable of the word in (almost all of) the Sogeram daughter languages, Mum among them, and Proto-Sogeram is reconstructed with word-final stress. The Mum data are Daniels' own January-February 2006 field wordlists (p. 165). Sec. 4.6 'Mum innovations' (pp. 178-179) gives only the phoneme inventory and segmental changes, with no separate stress remark for Mum.
new_statements.exceptions: None named; the hedge 'almost always word-final in the daughter languages' implies unspecified exceptions somewhere in the family, but the paper does not say which language or which words.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe Mum (Daniels' preferred name; Z'graggen's 'Katiati', Ethnologue kqa) as one language; no dialect is singled out for the stress statement. Daniels 2020 p. 74 notes a possible dialectal difference in transcription of *z (Sweeney <z> vs Daniels <j>), which is segmental, not prosodic. The 2010 stress sentence is about 'the daughter languages' of Proto-Sogeram collectively (Nend, Manat, Mum, Apalɨ, Sirva, Aisi, Kulsab, Atemple), not Mum alone.

sources.citation: Daniels, Don R. 2015. A Reconstruction of Proto-Sogeram: Phonology, Lexicon, and Morphosyntax. PhD dissertation, University of California, Santa Barbara. 1127 pp. (Mum: sec. 2.3.5 'Mum Innovations', printed pp. 93-96; research history p. 11; refs p. 1099)
sources.note: Nothing for Mum: sec. 2.3.5 gives the Mum phoneme inventory, word-final labiovelar creation, word-initial *i fortition and 'sporadic vowel centering' (penultimate-syllable *V > ɨ) with no statement on stress, accent or tone. Only stress remark in the work is p. 71 (Mand): 'Further research into the stress systems of the Sogeram languages might reveal a consistent pattern.' No Mum grammar sketch among the appendices. Names Sweeney 1994a as the (unpublished) Mum phonology.
